sermon:
## Go, Take a Wife of Whoredom
*God turns a prophet's marriage into a sermon Israel cannot walk out of*

**Text:** Hosea 1–3 · **Supporting:** Exodus 34:6–7 · Jeremiah 31:32 · Ezekiel 16:8 · Romans 5:8

God's first word to Hosea is not a doctrine. It is a command that wrecks a man's life.

**The Marriage God Ordered Broken**
"When the LORD first spoke through Hosea, the LORD said to Hosea, 'Go, take to yourself a wife of whoredom and have children of whoredom, for the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD'" (Hosea 1:2). Read that slowly. God tells a holy man to marry a woman who will betray him, and to do it knowing she will. The Hebrew under the whole book is *zanah* — to whore, the prophets' word for covenant betrayal — and God uses Hosea's own marriage bed as the pulpit. He could have sent a sermon. He sent a marriage. He could have written a treatise on idolatry; instead he made a man feel it in his own house, year after year, so that when Hosea finally opened his mouth, the grief in his voice would be real and not rhetorical. Then the children come, and their names are sentences God hangs around their necks. Jezreel, for the blood God will avenge in the valley. Lo-ruhamah, "No Mercy," because "I will no more have mercy on the house of Israel" (Hosea 1:6). Lo-ammi, "Not My People" — and the verdict lands in the nursery: "for you are not my people, and I am not your God" (Hosea 1:9). Every time Hosea calls his own children in from the field, he is preaching judgment with their names.

This was never about one man's domestic grief. The marriage God set up at Sinai — "my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, declares the LORD" (Jeremiah 31:32) — has been violated, and Hosea is made to feel in his own house what God has felt for four hundred years. We have softened idolatry into a category error. A theological mistake. A doctrinal slip we correct with better teaching. God refuses the softening. He calls it adultery, and adultery is not an idea. It is a wife in another man's bed while her husband waits up.

**The God Who Counts the Gifts She Gave Away**
Then chapter 2 opens the husband's case, and it is unbearable, because it is tender. "And she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil, and who lavished on her silver and gold, which they used for Baal" (Hosea 2:8). The cruelest detail in the whole prophecy is that small one. He paid for the gifts she handed to her lovers. Every good thing she used to chase Baal had come from the husband she was chasing him to spite. The grain she offered on a pagan altar grew in his fields. The silver she melted into an idol came from his hand. Ezekiel preaches the same wound — God spreading his garment over a naked, abandoned girl, washing her, clothing her, entering into covenant with her (Ezekiel 16:8) — only to watch her take the jewelry he gave her and spend it on strangers.

And what does this God threaten? "Therefore I will hedge up her way with thorns, and I will build a wall against her, so that she cannot find her paths" (Hosea 2:6). He hedges her road with thorns not to abandon her but to exhaust her, until the lovers cannot satisfy and she says, "I will go and return to my first husband, for it was better for me then than now" (Hosea 2:7). The judgment is the mercy. The wall is built by love. He makes her chosen path painful precisely so that the path home looks like home again. I have sat in a counseling office across from a man who was doing the math of every gift he gave his wife that she spent on someone else, and I had no words for him. I have also been Gomer. So have you. We took the marriage and the breath and the years and the daily bread, and we spent every bit of it on lesser gods, and we called it freedom. The hedge of thorns God put across our easy roads — the illness, the loss, the wall we keep hitting — we called it bad luck. It was a husband building a wall to bring his wife home.

**The Silver That Buys Back a Whore**
Chapter 3 is the gospel acted out in a slave market. Gomer has sunk so far that she is no longer being chased — she is being sold. And God says to Hosea: "Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel" (Hosea 3:1). Not a stranger. *Again.* The same woman, who used every kindness against him, who shamed his name in the town, now standing on an auction block with a price on her head. And Hosea pays. "So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley" (Hosea 3:2). He gathers up cash and grain — half the price of an ordinary slave, scraped together because that is all she is worth now — and he buys his own wife back from the ruin she chose for herself. He does not buy a new bride. He buys back the old one, at a discount, because adultery had made her cheap.

This is the hinge of the entire book, and it is the shadow of a darker market and a higher price. Where Hosea spent silver and barley, Christ spent himself. "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). Not after we cleaned up. Not once we were worth it. While we were still on the block. The husband at Sinai who proclaimed himself "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6) did not finally redeem his bride with coins. He redeemed her with a cross, buying back the very people who drove the nails. Hosea could only act it out with a borrowed bag of barley. Christ accomplished it with his own blood.

The question Hosea leaves in the room is not whether God is angry. It is why a God this betrayed would still send a man to the market with money in his hand. And if you have ever been the one sold, and bought back anyway, you already know it does not feel like justice. It feels like being loved past the point where you deserved to be.

He bought back what betrayed him.

## The LORD Has a Case Against the Land
*When the people who were paid to know God grow rich off the people who don't*

**Text:** Hosea 4 · **Supporting:** Malachi 2:7 · Isaiah 5:13 · Jeremiah 5:31 · 1 Timothy 4:16

God does not lose his temper in Hosea 4. He files suit.

**The Indictment Read Into the Record**
"Hear the word of the LORD, O children of Israel, for the LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of the land. There is no faithfulness or steadfast love, and no knowledge of God in the land" (Hosea 4:1). The word translated "controversy" is a courtroom word — *rib*, a covenant lawsuit, the offended party rising in the assembly to lay out the breach. This is not a tantrum. It is a legal action, and God has the standing to bring it because he is the wronged party to the covenant. The charge sheet is three absences. No faithfulness. No steadfast love — *chesed*, the covenant loyalty a husband and wife owe each other. No knowledge of God in the land at all.

Then the fruit of those absences: "there is swearing, lying, murder, stealing, and committing adultery; they break all bounds, and bloodshed follows bloodshed" (Hosea 4:2). Read those two verses together and the order matters more than anything else in the chapter. The murder and the lying are not the disease. They are the symptoms. The disease named first is that a nation has stopped knowing its God, and a people who do not know God will eventually do anything to each other. The bloodshed in the streets is downstream of the emptiness in the sanctuary. We keep treating the symptoms. We legislate against the bloodshed and moralize against the lying and run programs against the stealing, and we wonder why the next generation is harder than the last. Isaiah named it long before Hosea's lawsuit was filed: "Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge" (Isaiah 5:13). Not for lack of religion. Not for lack of activity. For lack of God.

**The Shepherds Who Eat the Sheep**
Then God turns to the men who were supposed to fix this, and the prophecy gets specific in a way that should make every pastor in the room flinch. "My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge; because you have rejected knowledge, I reject you from being a priest to me" (Hosea 4:6). The "you" goes singular. The priest. The man God appointed to stand between the people and himself, the man whose whole vocation was to carry the knowledge of God to a people who could not reach it on their own. Malachi will state the job description plainly — "the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts" (Malachi 2:7) — but Hosea's priests have done the precise opposite of their office. They have rejected the very knowledge they were ordained to guard.

And here is the line that turns the stomach, the line you almost never hear preached: "They feed on the sin of my people; they are greedy for their iniquity" (Hosea 4:8). The clergy have found a way to profit from the people's falling. Under the sacrificial system, more sin meant more sin offerings brought to the altar, and more offerings meant more meat on the priest's table. They had a financial stake in the congregation staying broken. The worse the people got, the better the priests ate. Jeremiah saw the same arrangement running in his day: "the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule at their direction; my people love to have it so" (Jeremiah 5:31). A corrupt clergy and a congregation that prefers it that way — they deserve each other, and they destroy each other.

I am a pastor. I cannot preach this chapter from outside it. The temptation to flatter the people who fund the work, to keep the diagnosis vague so the giving stays warm, to make "lack of knowledge" a problem out there in the pews and never up here behind the pulpit — I know that temptation by name, because I have felt it reach for me from inside my own ministry. There is a quiet, respectable way to feed on the sin of God's people: tell them what they want, keep the hard word soft, and let the platform grow. Paul's charge to Timothy is a knife pointed at the man holding it: "Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this" (1 Timothy 4:16). On yourself first. The watchman is watched.

**The Verdict That Falls on the Watchman**
What does God do with leaders who profit from the perishing? "And it shall be like people, like priest" (Hosea 4:9). The leader does not float above the judgment of the led. He is dragged down inside it, because he built the trap they fell into. And the result is a whole nation moving through its religious motions while the knowledge of God quietly drains out of it: "a people without understanding shall come to ruin" (Hosea 4:14). Full altars, empty hearts, and a clergy growing fat on the difference.

This is exactly where Christ stands over the chapter, because Christ is the one priest who did not eat his people's sin. He bore it. The Good Shepherd does not feed on the sheep; he lays down his life for them, the very inversion of Hosea 4. Where the false priest grew rich on iniquity, the true High Priest was made poor by it, made sin by it, crucified by it — and he bought the flock anyway, with his own blood, the flock that perished for lack of the knowledge he came to be. Every greedy priest in Hosea 4 is the dark negative of the One who knew the cost of the people's sin and paid it himself instead of charging them for it.

So the lawsuit is still open, and it is not only Israel's. It is the open question hanging over every pulpit, including the one I stand in: are the people perishing for lack of knowledge, and am I living off the perishing?

My people perish for ignorance.

## Your Love Is Like a Morning Cloud
*The repentance that means it only until the danger passes*

**Text:** Hosea 6:1–11 · **Supporting:** 1 Samuel 15:22 · Micah 6:6–8 · Matthew 9:13 · Psalm 51:17

Hosea 6 opens with a prayer so good you would put it on a worship slide. God is not impressed.

**The Confession That Sounds Right**
Listen to it: "Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up" (Hosea 6:1). Every word is theologically correct. They have the doctrine of divine discipline — he tore us *that he may heal*. They have the confidence of grace. They even have what sounds like resurrection language: "After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him" (Hosea 6:2). If a member of your congregation prayed this aloud, you would weep with relief and put their name on the prayer chain as a testimony. The doctrine is sound. The cadence is beautiful. And then the very next line tells you what is wrong with the whole thing: "Let us know; let us press on to know the LORD" (Hosea 6:3).

The words are flawless. The heart behind them is a weather forecast. *Let us press on* — the language of a people who have learned the right liturgy of return and can recite it on cue whenever the pressure rises and the enemy gets close. We have built whole revival meetings on Hosea 6:1–3 and stopped reading at verse 4. Stop there and it is a hymn. Keep reading and it is an autopsy. The prayer was never the problem. God can read what is under it, and what is under this one is a people who have figured out that the right words can buy them out of the consequences without ever costing them the marriage.

**The God Who Watches the Cloud Burn Off**
Because God answers the prayer, and his answer is grief. "What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? Your love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away" (Hosea 6:4). There is the diagnosis, and it is not anger — it is a husband at the window watching the fog lift. Their *chesed*, their covenant love, is real at dawn and gone by noon. It is not that they were lying when they prayed. It is that they meant every word for exactly as long as the danger lasted, and danger does not last. Sincerity that evaporates is still evaporation. The tears were wet. By afternoon they were dry, and so was the devotion.

So God tells them what he was actually after the whole time, behind all the sacrifices they kept bringing: "For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings" (Hosea 6:6). There is the heartbeat of the prophets in a single line. Samuel said it to Saul standing in a field of plunder — "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams" (1 Samuel 15:22). Micah asked the question every religious person asks — what does the LORD want, more offerings, more rivers of oil, the firstborn? — and answered it flat: "to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8). God was never running a sacrifice-collection business. He was after the marriage. He wanted to be *known* — not appeased, not paid, *known* — and Israel kept handing him liturgy instead of loyalty, ritual instead of relationship, the form of return without the fact of it.

I know how to perform repentance. I have prayed the right prayer with the right tears at the right altar in the right crisis, and then watched my own devotion burn off by Tuesday afternoon — the dew gone, the cloud lifted, the God I wept toward on Sunday quietly demoted somewhere around Wednesday lunch without my even noticing the demotion. That is the morning cloud, and I am describing the inside of my own chest, not Ephraim's. I cannot point at this nation. I am this nation. So are you. You have prayed a Hosea 6:1 prayer that was bone dry by noon, and you know it.

**The Knowledge God Came to Have With Us**
Here is the turn the chapter is built toward. The God who refuses morning-cloud devotion is the same God who, centuries later, sat down at a tax collector's table and quoted this exact verse back at the men who thought their sacrifices made them clean. When the religious crowd sneered at the company he was keeping, Jesus said, "Go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice'" (Matthew 9:13). Hosea 6:6, on the lips of the Bridegroom, aimed at the people most confident in their own repentance. Christ did not come to collect more sacrifices from people who repent only until the crisis passes. He came to *be* the steadfast love that Israel could never produce — the *chesed* that does not burn off, the loyalty that held when ours fled, the one whose love for the Father did not evaporate at noon on a Friday outside the city wall when the sky went dark. He is the morning cloud that did not lift. He stayed.

And the only repentance that is not a morning cloud is the one David named from the floor, after the worst night of his life: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17). Not a forecast. A funeral for the old self. So the question Hosea hands you is not whether you can pray the right prayer. You just heard one that was perfect. The question is whether it will still be true at noon — and that question should make every one of us who knows all the right words go very quiet.

Your repentance evaporates by noon.

## They Sow the Wind
*A nation discovers it cannot call back a harvest it already planted*

**Text:** Hosea 8 · **Supporting:** Galatians 6:7 · Job 4:8 · Proverbs 22:8 · Psalm 20:7

There is a kind of judgment God does not have to send. He only has to let the seed come up.

**The Kings and Calves of Their Own Making**
Hosea 8 names two acts of manufacture, and both are Israel reaching for a god small enough to control. First the politics: "They made kings, but not through me. They set up princes, but I knew it not" (Hosea 8:4). The northern kingdom in Hosea's own lifetime was a slaughterhouse of thrones — kings crowned by assassination, dynasties rising and falling in a single year, a nation seizing power instead of receiving it from the only One who gives it. They wanted a strong man on the throne and they did not much care how he got there. Then the religion, running on the exact same self-made logic: "With their silver and gold they made idols for their own destruction" (Hosea 8:4). And the golden calf at Samaria, which God treats with open, withering contempt: "A craftsman made it; it is not God. The calf of Samaria shall be broken to pieces" (Hosea 8:6). They wanted strength they could see and a god they could carry in their arms, so they trusted the things their own hands had built.

Israel had been warned a thousand years where that trust ends. "Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7). They chose the chariot. They always do. So do we, when we trust the thing we manufactured to save us — the savings account we built, the strongman we elected, the platform we grew, the reputation we constructed brick by brick — over the God who cannot be carried, cannot be controlled, and cannot be voted into office. The calf at Samaria looked like security. It was a cow made of melted-down jewelry, and a craftsman made it.

**The Law of the Harvest**
And then comes the verse the whole sermon turns on, eight words that govern the moral universe: "For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind" (Hosea 8:7). This is not arbitrary punishment dropped on a nation from a clear sky. It is agriculture. It is the most reliable law God built into creation, and Paul stated it bare and unblinking: "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). The wisdom tradition had it long before Paul — Job's friend: "those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same" (Job 4:8); the proverb: "whoever sows injustice will reap calamity" (Proverbs 22:8). The principle is old, it is fixed, and it does not negotiate.

Israel thought it could plant rebellion and harvest security. Sow self-made kings and self-made gods and somehow gather peace at the end of the season. But the wind they scattered did not blow away and vanish. Wind gathers. It organizes itself into a storm, and a storm has a name, and the name this time is Assyria. "The standing grain has no heads; it shall yield no flour; if it were to yield, strangers would devour it" (Hosea 8:7). The harvest fails outright, and the little that comes up feeds the invader. Israel did not just risk Assyria. Israel planted it — every faithless treaty, every self-crowned king, every calf — and now stood in the field watching it ripen.

I would like to believe my private compromises stay private. That what I sow in the dark does not come up in the daylight. Hosea 8 says it germinates. The small dishonesties I told myself were nothing, the chariots I quietly trust instead of God, the kings of my own making that I crowned without ever telling him — I sowed those, every one, and I do not get to vote on the harvest. None of us does. We mock God in the planting, certain there will be no reaping, and then we stand stunned at the whirlwind as if it had nothing to do with us — as if the storm were weather and not crop.

**The One Who Reaped What He Did Not Sow**
But press the law of the harvest all the way to the cross, and something breaks open in it. Christ is the one man in all of history who sowed only righteousness — and reaped the whirlwind anyway. He planted perfect obedience and harvested a crown of thorns. He scattered nothing but mercy and gathered the full wrath that was ours to reap. The God who is not mocked let himself be mocked — spat on, struck, stripped, and crucified — reaping a storm he never once sowed, so that we could be spared the harvest we planted with both hands. That is the only exit from Galatians 6:7 that has ever existed. Not a loophole in the law of sowing and reaping, because God will not be mocked and the law holds. A Substitute standing in our field, taking our whirlwind into his own body, so that the seed we scattered breaks over his head and not ours.

So the wind you are scattering today is not lost in the air. It is on its way back to you, gathering weight as it comes, and the only question that finally matters is whether that storm breaks over your head or over his.

They sowed wind. The whirlwind comes.

## When Israel Was a Child I Loved Him
*The holy God who cannot make himself give the rebel up*

**Text:** Hosea 11:1–11 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 1:31 · Matthew 2:15 · Isaiah 49:15 · Lamentations 3:22

For ten chapters God has been the offended Husband. In chapter 11 he becomes the heartbroken Father, and the prophecy nearly stops breathing.

**The Father Who Taught Him to Walk**
"When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son" (Hosea 11:1). The whole tone of the book shifts here. This is not a courtroom and not a slave market; it is a father going through old memories. And what God remembers is not Israel's strength or Israel's glory but Israel's infancy — the small, helpless, learning-to-stand years, before the rebellion, when the nation was a toddler holding on with both hands. "Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk; I took them up by their arms" (Hosea 11:3). Picture it, because God means for you to picture it. The Almighty bent all the way down, holding a stumbling nation by both wrists, steadying its first steps across the floor. "I led them with cords of kindness, with the bands of love, and I became to them as one who eases the yoke on their jaws, and I bent down to them and fed them" (Hosea 11:4). I bent down. I fed him by hand. Moses had reached for the same picture at the edge of the wilderness — "in the wilderness, where you have seen how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went" (Deuteronomy 1:31).

And the wound underneath the memory is the line that ends the verse: "but they did not know that I healed them" (Hosea 11:3). The child grew up and forgot whose hands had held him, whose arms had carried him, whose patience had taught him to walk. He took the legs God gave him and used them to walk away.

I was raised without a father, and I cannot read Hosea 11 from a safe distance, and I will not pretend to. The God who bends down to teach a child to walk is describing the exact thing the fatherless ache for in the dark and the exact thing every human father — including me, with my five sons — fails to do perfectly however hard he tries. This is not sentiment, and it is not a warm illustration. This is the deepest hunger in the human chest, the absence that organizes a whole life around itself, and God stands in Hosea 11 and claims to be its answer. Not a substitute for the missing father. The Father the missing one was always a broken copy of.

**The War Inside God**
Then justice speaks, and justice is not wrong. The child has rebelled — has run to Assyria, has burned incense to idols, has spent every gift on Baal — and the sentence is just: "The sword shall rage against their cities, consume the bars of their gates, and devour them" (Hosea 11:6). By every standard of covenant law God has written, he should hand Ephraim over and walk away clean. The verdict would be righteous.

And here the prophecy does something almost unbearable. It lets us hear God argue with himself. "How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel? How can I make you like Admah? How can I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender" (Hosea 11:8). Admah and Zeboiim were the cities destroyed alongside Sodom — God is saying, how can I do to my son what I did to the cities of the plain? The word for "recoils" is the language of being overturned, churned, convulsed — the very verb used for the *overthrow* of Sodom is here turned inward. What God did to those cities, his own heart now does to itself rather than do it to his child.

And then the line that explains the entire Bible: "I will not execute my burning anger; I will not again destroy Ephraim; for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not come in wrath" (Hosea 11:9). Read it twice, because it does not say what we expect. We expect God to say his love overrides his holiness, that mercy wins by suspending the rules. He says the opposite. He will not destroy *because* he is the Holy One — his holiness is the reason he refuses to give the rebel up. A man, wronged like this, would have walked, and called the walking justice. God's very holiness is what will not abandon. Isaiah reaches for the same impossibility: "Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you" (Isaiah 49:15). It is "the steadfast love of the LORD" that "never ceases; his mercies never come to an end" (Lamentations 3:22).

**The Son Who Made the Memory True**
But how can a holy God refuse to execute burning anger on a guilty people and still be holy? Hosea 11 raises that question with everything it has and cannot answer it. The New Testament can. Matthew takes the very first line of this chapter — "out of Egypt I called my son" — and lays it on the infant Christ being carried home from Egypt by Joseph and Mary: "This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, 'Out of Egypt I called my son'" (Matthew 2:15). Israel was the son who failed every step of the way out of Egypt. Jesus is the Son who did not fail a single step. And on the cross, the burning anger that God refused to execute on Ephraim was executed in full — on the faithful Son, in the place of the faithless one. That is how the holiness that would not give up the rebel and the justice that demanded payment meet without either being denied. God did not lower the bar in Hosea 11. He held it, and then paid it himself, in his own Son, so that his compassion could grow warm and tender without his righteousness growing cold.

So the question Hosea 11 leaves hanging — how can God not give us up? — has a name now, and the name is Jesus. And if you have ever been the child who forgot whose hands held you, who took the legs you were given and walked away, the only honest response is to stand still and wonder why, after all of it, those hands are still open.

His mercy overruled his wrath.

## I Will Be Your Death, O Death
*The hand that strikes the nation is the only hand that can raise the dead*

**Text:** Hosea 13 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 15:54–55 · Deuteronomy 8:11–14 · Job 5:18 · Revelation 1:18

Hosea 13 is the darkest chapter in the book, and it is where the resurrection first speaks.

**The Sin of Being Full**
God begins by naming a sin we almost never preach against, because we are busy committing it. "When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel, but he incurred guilt through Baal and died" (Hosea 13:1). A people that once trembled before God is now spiritually dead — and the cause is not what you would guess. How did a trembling people die? Not through famine. Not through persecution. Through plenty. "But when they had grazed, they became full, they were filled, and their heart was lifted up; therefore they forgot me" (Hosea 13:6). They ate until they were satisfied, and satisfaction made them proud, and pride made them forgetful, and forgetting God is the death itself.

This is the exact danger Moses stood and warned about at the very edge of the promised land, before they had eaten a single fat meal in it: "Take care lest you forget the LORD your God... lest, when you have eaten and are full, and have built good houses and live in them, and when your herds and flocks multiply... then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 8:11–14). The wilderness, where God fed them by hand with manna, had produced dependence. The good land, where they fed themselves off full barns, produced amnesia. "It was I who knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought" (Hosea 13:5) — I held you when you were hungry, and you forgot me the moment you were full.

I am most spiritually careless not when life is hard but when it is comfortable. I pray hardest in the crisis and coast through the calm. So do you. The full stomach is more dangerous to faith than the empty one, and a well-fed people is the easiest people on earth to lose, because they cannot feel themselves drifting. We did not forget God in the storm. We forgot him at the buffet — somewhere between the second house and the full retirement account, the trembling stopped, and we never noticed when.

**The Lion God**
So the gentle Father of chapter 11 — the one who bent down to teach Ephraim to walk — now describes himself in terms meant to make us tremble again. "So I am to them like a lion; like a leopard I will lurk beside the way. I will fall upon them like a bear robbed of her cubs; I will tear open their breast" (Hosea 13:7–8). This is not cruelty, and it is not a different God than chapter 11. This is the same love refusing to let his people drift comfortably and quietly into death without a fight. He becomes the lion in the road precisely because he will not stand by and watch the people he taught to walk wander off a cliff while patting their full stomachs. Even Job's friend, so often wrong, spoke truth here: "For he wounds, but he binds up; he shatters, but his hands heal" (Job 5:18). The wounding and the healing are the same hands.

And then, at the very bottom of the chapter, in the middle of a death sentence, comes the most astonishing reversal in all the prophets: "Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol? Shall I redeem them from Death? O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?" (Hosea 13:14). The same God who came as the lion now speaks of plundering the grave itself, of calling out death's own plagues to do his bidding. The hand that strikes is the only hand in the universe that can reach down into Sheol and pull a dead people back out of it. Judgment and resurrection in the same breath, from the same mouth, by the same hand.

**The Sting Drawn Out**
And this is the verse the apostle Paul could not leave alone. Standing in spirit over the empty tomb in his great resurrection chapter, Paul reaches all the way back to Hosea 13 and turns the question into a taunt flung at a defeated enemy: "Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?" (1 Corinthians 15:54–55). What Hosea spoke as a haunting question buried in a chapter of judgment, Christ turned into a settled fact buried in an empty grave. The God who said "I will be your death, O Death" made good on it by dying — by going down into Sheol himself, taking its full plague and sting into his own body on the cross, and walking back out the other side with the keys on his belt.

The risen Christ says it in his own words, to a terrified disciple on Patmos: "Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades" (Revelation 1:18). The lion of Hosea 13 is the Lamb who was slain. The same hand that fell on Israel like a bear robbed of her cubs is the hand now pierced and raised and holding the keys to the grave. So you are not asked to choose between a God who strikes and a God who saves. Hosea 13 will not let you split them. They are one God, one hand, one love — and the only hope a full, forgetful, dying people has is that the hand strong enough to wound is the hand strong enough to raise the dead.

The hand that strikes can raise.

## Return, O Israel
*The book ends not with a verdict but with an open door, and God holds it himself*

**Text:** Hosea 14 · **Supporting:** Luke 15:20–22 · Ezekiel 36:26 · John 15:5 · Romans 2:4

Thirteen chapters of indictment, adultery, lawsuit, lion, and grave — and Hosea ends with God teaching his unfaithful wife the very words to come home.

**The Repentance God Writes for You**
"Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled because of your iniquity" (Hosea 14:1). After everything — after the whoredom and the lawsuit and the whirlwind and the bear robbed of her cubs — the door is still open. But look at the strange mercy in what comes next, because it is the gospel hiding in plain sight. God does not stand back and wait to see whether Israel can compose a confession worthy of being heard. He writes the confession for them. "Take with you words and return to the LORD; say to him, 'Take away all iniquity; accept what is good, and we will pay with bulls the vows of our lips'" (Hosea 14:2). The God who was betrayed dictates the apology of the betrayer. He puts the words of return into the mouth that wronged him.

And the heart of the prayer he writes is the renunciation of every false savior the book has spent thirteen chapters exposing: "Assyria shall not save us; we will not ride on horses; and we will say no more, 'Our God,' to the work of our own hands" (Hosea 14:3). No more Assyria, the foreign treaty. No more horses, the military strength. No more calling a thing we built ourselves "our God." The repentance God puts in their mouths is the surrender of every idol they ever reached for in order to avoid him — the chariot, the king, the calf, all of it laid down at once. This is exactly what Paul means when he says "the kindness of God is meant to lead you to repentance" (Romans 2:4). Even the words of our return are a gift from the One we are returning to.

**Love Freely, Without a Price**
And then God answers his own prayer with a sentence that changes the entire register of the book in a single line: "I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them" (Hosea 14:4). Sit on that one word — *freely*. For thirteen chapters God has been the husband demanding the bride price, the prosecutor pressing the lawsuit, the lion guarding the road, the bear tearing the breast. Now: freely. No restitution. No probation. No bulls required after all, despite what the dictated prayer offered — the offering was never the point. The verb is the pure language of gift. He is no longer the offended Husband collecting on a debt. He has become the dew.

"I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon" (Hosea 14:5). Dew is not earned and dew is not summoned. It falls in the night while the field sleeps, on the just and the unjust alike, and a nation that went to bed withered wakes up green. This is the new heart that Ezekiel was promised in exile: "And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26). And it is the father in the parable, who saw his ruined son "while he was still a long way off" and "ran and embraced him and kissed him" before the boy could even finish the speech he had rehearsed all the way home, calling for the best robe and the ring and the fattened calf (Luke 15:20–22). The son had words ready. The father did not wait to hear them.

I have rehearsed my way back to God like a man preparing a legal defense, certain I had to earn the right to enter the room before the door would open. Every single time, the door was already open, and I had spent the whole walk home distrusting the very welcome that was waiting for me. So have you. We keep trying to pay for what God has already decided to give freely, as if our payment honored him — as if the bulls made the grace more respectable — when in fact our insistence on paying only insults the gift and slanders the Giver.

**The Fruit That Comes From Him Alone**
And the last great line of the prophecy locates the whole of our fruitfulness completely outside ourselves: "O Ephraim, what have I to do with idols? It is I who answer and look after you. I am like an evergreen cypress; from me comes your fruit" (Hosea 14:8). From me comes your fruit. Not from your effort, not from your repentance, not from your bulls or your vows or your white-knuckle resolve to do better this time — from me. The cypress does not ask the branch to manufacture its own life. Centuries later the Bridegroom himself would say it again with his own face turned toward his friends: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing" (John 15:5).

The Hosea who bought back his wife with silver and a bag of barley was always pointing here — to the One who would heal apostasy not by demanding payment but by becoming the very source of the life he asks of us, redeeming the unfaithful at the cost of himself and then growing them green from his own roots. The book that opened with "Go, take a wife of whoredom" ends with a wife made fruitful by the Husband she betrayed, blossoming like a lily because the dew finally fell.

So Hosea closes with no verdict. After thirteen chapters of them, it ends instead with a question still standing in the doorway: "Whoever is wise, let him understand these things; whoever is discerning, let him know them" (Hosea 14:9). The door is open. The words of return have already been written for you. The only thing left undone in the entire book is the walking through it.

Return. He is the healing.
